purpose: Potassium is a natural mineral your body needs to keep your heart, muscles, and nerves working properly. Your doctor may prescribe it if your potassium levels are too low, which can happen from taking certain water pills (diuretics), vomiting, or not getting enough from your diet. Keeping your potassium at the right level helps prevent muscle weakness, cramps, and heart rhythm problems.
how_it_works: Potassium is an important mineral that your body's cells use to send electrical signals, especially in the heart and muscles. When your levels are low, your heart and muscles don't get the signals they need to work correctly. Taking a potassium supplement simply restores and maintains that balance so everything runs smoothly.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or an upset stomach. Taking it with food or a full glass of water can help reduce these. Some people notice a mild stomach ache, especially if they take it on an empty stomach.
warnings: Too much potassium can be dangerous and cause a serious, life-threatening heart rhythm problem, so never take more than prescribed. Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, since your kidneys may not remove extra potassium well. Also let your doctor know about all other medications you take, especially ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics, as these can raise your potassium levels even higher.
typical_dosing: The dose varies widely depending on your needs, but a common adult dose is 20 to 40 milliequivalents (mEq) per day, taken in divided doses with meals and a full glass of water. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never crush or chew extended-release tablets — swallow them whole.
